stem: When was the Rowlatt Act passed?
expl: To curb the rising revolutionary activities in India, the government constituted a committee in 1917 under the chairmanship of Justice Sidney Rowlatt, with the objective of preparing an effective plan to suppress terrorism. On the basis of its recommendations, the bill passed in March, 1919 came to be known as the Rowlatt Act. Under the Rowlatt Act, the British government could imprison anyone, without trial, for a maximum of two years. Therefore, this law was called the law of “No appeal, No dalil, No Vakil”.

expl: In view of the growing opposition to the Rowlatt Act, the government imposed a ban on Gandhiji and some other leaders from entering Punjab. This increased public anger there. The anger grew further when two popular leaders of Punjab—Dr. Satyapal and Dr. Kitchlew—were arrested. To protest this arrest and the Rowlatt Act, people organised a huge meeting at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. In the same garden, on 13 April, 1919, Brigadier General Dyer carried out a brutal massacre during a peaceful public meeting.

expl: After the heart-rending incident of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on 13 April, 1919, Rabindranath Tagore returned the ‘Knighthood’ title conferred by the British Crown. Tagore said— “The time has come when medals of honour make our shame glaring in the absurd context of humiliation; as for me, I wish to stand by my countrymen, stripped of all special titles.”

stem: Who viewed the Khilafat Movement as an opportunity for integrating Hindus and Muslims which will not appear again within coming hundred years?
expl: On 23–24 November, 1919, the All-India Khilafat Conference was held in Delhi, and Gandhiji was its president (on 24 November). In December, 1919, the Khilafat Movement received further support at the Amritsar Session of the Indian National Congress. Until then, the Congress had carefully kept itself separate from religious matters; but after the Khilafat Movement began, Gandhiji felt that this was a golden opportunity to unite Hindus and Muslims—an opportunity that might not be available again even in the next hundred years.

stem: In which city was the conference of Khilafat Committee in 1920 held that requested Gandhiji to assume the leadership of Non-Cooperation Movement?
expl: Gandhiji advised the Khilafat Committee in 1920 to launch a Non-Cooperation Movement against British rule. In June, 1920, the Khilafat Committee accepted this advice at Allahabad (Now – Prayagraj) and authorised Gandhiji to lead the movement. In September, 1920, at the special session of the Congress held in Calcutta under the leadership of Lala Lajpat Rai, the decision to launch the Non-Cooperation Movement was taken.

stem: Why did Mahatma Gandhi support the Khilafat Movement?

options.label: a
options.text: The Khalifa had given shelter to Indian revolutionaries

options.label: b
options.text: Gandhiji wanted to win the support of the Indian Muslims against the British

options.label: c
options.text: The Khalifa supported Indian struggle for freedom

options.label: d
options.text: The Khalifa was a friend of Gandhiji

expl: The Khilafat Movement began against the British plan to partition the Turkish (Ottoman) Empire. On 23–24 November, 1919, at the All-India Khilafat Conference held in Delhi, Gandhiji was made the president of the conference on 24 November, 1919. The Khilafat Movement received further momentum from the Amritsar Session of the Indian National Congress in December, 1919. Gandhiji saw it as a golden opportunity for Hindu–Muslim unity—one that might not be available even in the next hundred years. Therefore, he supported the Khilafat Movement to secure the cooperation of Indian Muslims in the struggle against the British.

stem: Which event served as a catalyst for the Khilafat Movement?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: The immediate issue of the Khilafat Movement was the fear that, after the First World War, harsh peace terms would be imposed on the Ottoman Empire, and the protection of the position and powers of the Khalifa (Caliph), who was highly respected in the Muslim world. In this context, the Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March, 1919. Supporters of the Khilafat believed that the Allied Powers would deal leniently with the Ottoman Empire; but the humiliating Treaty of Versailles signed by the Allies with Germany in June, 1919 shattered this belief. As a result, the Khilafat Movement intensified in India to protect Turkey’s holy places and the office of the Khalifa. Although the Treaty of Versailles was not directly related to the Ottoman Empire, it influenced the Khilafat Movement in India by affecting opinions regarding the Khalifa's position and the future of the Ottoman Empire.
